narrative.text: The Russian-language cover of the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework for the sharing of influenza viruses and access to vaccines and other benefits.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The Russian title page of the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework.
The cataloguing and copyright page of the Russian edition, with English WHO library cataloguing data and subject headings and Russian rights, permissions and disclaimer notices.

The first page of the Russian table of contents of the PIP Framework, listing resolution WHA64.5, principles, objective, scope, definitions, the virus-sharing system and early benefit-sharing sections. It runs up to the provision of diagnostic reagents and test kits.

Continues the Russian table of contents, listing benefit-sharing sections on reference reagents, capacity building, stockpiles, pricing, technology transfer and financing, governance and review, and the annexes on material transfer agreements and terms of reference.

Presents in Russian resolution WHA64.5 of the Sixty-fourth World Health Assembly (24 May 2011), which considers the open-ended working group's report and adopts the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework and its annexes. It urges Member States to implement and support the Framework and calls on stakeholders to give it priority.

Concludes resolution WHA64.5, asking the Director-General, with the Advisory Group, to implement and monitor the Framework and report every two years to the Health Assembly through the Executive Board.

Begins the principles of the PIP Framework in Russian, recalling resolution WHA60.28 and the continuing threat of an influenza pandemic, especially to developing countries. It affirms Member States' commitment to share H5N1 and other potentially pandemic viruses and their benefits on an equal footing and in line with the International Health Regulations (2005).

Continues the principles, recognizing the need for a fair, transparent and effective system for sharing viruses and benefits, WHO's leadership, sovereign rights over biological resources and the global strategy on innovation and intellectual property. It also notes concern over insufficient vaccine production capacity and that some Member States cannot develop, produce or afford vaccines.

Concludes the principles by noting WHO's Global Pandemic Influenza Action Plan to raise vaccine production capacity, the need for technology transfer to developing countries and financing mechanisms for affordable, equitable access to vaccines and technologies.

States the Framework's objective of improving pandemic influenza preparedness and response by strengthening the WHO surveillance network to achieve fair and equitable sharing of viruses and access to vaccines and other benefits.
Defines the Framework's scope as the sharing of H5N1 and other potentially pandemic influenza viruses and related benefits, excluding seasonal viruses and other pathogens in shared specimens.

Opens the Russian definitions section, defining PIP biological materials as human clinical specimens, wild-type virus isolates, modified candidate vaccine viruses and related RNA and cDNA. It also defines terms such as genetic sequence and notes the operational exemption for non-commercial public health use.

Defines further technical terms used in the Framework, such as potency testing reagents, influenza virus of human pandemic potential, PIP candidate vaccine virus, clinical specimens, reference viruses and WHO-recommended vaccine viruses.

Completes the definition of wild-type influenza viruses and defines the institutions involved, including essential regulatory laboratories, manufacturers, national influenza centres, other authorized laboratories, WHO collaborating centres and H5 reference laboratories.

Defines the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System and its component laboratories, followed by other terms such as Advisory Group, affected country, least developed countries, originating laboratory and Member State, traceability mechanism and the PIP stockpiles.

Opens the Russian section on the system for sharing H5N1 and other potentially pandemic viruses, under which Member States should rapidly provide PIP materials to WHO collaborating centres or H5 reference laboratories, consenting to onward transfer under the SMTAs. It also allows bilateral sharing if WHO laboratories are prioritized and begins the provisions on genetic sequence data.

Covers sharing of genetic sequence data within the WHO network and through public databases, noting sensitivities for some countries, and asks the Director-General to define a process for resolving related issues. It then describes the electronic traceability mechanism for PIP materials and allows temporary changes to recording requirements in a pandemic emergency.

Limits emergency changes to the traceability requirements to the relevant pandemic strains and requires the Director-General to report them. It also specifies that SMTA 1 covers transfers within the WHO network and SMTA 2 is used with entities outside it.

Opens the Russian section on the PIP benefit-sharing system, calling on Member States, WHO, manufacturers and researchers to support a system that provides all countries with surveillance, risk assessment and early warning. It prioritizes benefits such as antivirals and vaccines for developing and affected countries according to risk and need, along with capacity building.

Describes WHO's coordination of pandemic preparedness and response under the International Health Regulations, including fair allocation of scarce vaccines, antivirals and diagnostics during a pandemic. It also covers risk assessment and response, with network laboratories sharing analysis reports, and begins the provisions on supplying candidate vaccine viruses.

Specifies that candidate vaccine viruses go without preference to manufacturers, originating and other countries' laboratories and others, subject to biosafety rules. It also covers free diagnostic reagents and test kits, potency testing reagents for regulators and manufacturers, and support for building national laboratory and surveillance capacity.

Lists the aims of laboratory capacity building, such as rapid virus detection and characterization, participation in risk assessment and research. It then covers strengthening regulatory capacity, public information on product approvals and the WHO antiviral stockpile sustained through donations and expert guidance.

Sets out the WHO PIP vaccine stockpile of H5N1 and other pandemic vaccines with related equipment, initially 150 million doses, 50 million for affected countries to contain early outbreaks and 100 million for developing countries per capita once a pandemic begins. It covers donations from manufacturers, expert guidance on its management and financing if donations fall short, and opens the section on vaccines for developing countries between pandemics.

Asks Member States to urge manufacturers to reserve part of each production run of H5N1 and potentially pandemic vaccines for stockpiles or developing countries, and covers provision of pandemic vaccines and an expert process on international distribution mechanisms. It also calls for tiered pricing by country income and begins the provisions on technology transfer under the Global Pandemic Influenza Action Plan.

Asks Member States to urge manufacturers to transfer vaccine, diagnostic and pharmaceutical technologies to other countries, especially developing countries, and encourages those seeking production technology to study the burden of seasonal influenza first. It then sets out sustainable financing, including manufacturers' annual partnership contribution equal to half the WHO network's running costs, with a footnote explaining that the contribution will change as those costs change.

Explains in Russian that industry contributions to the pandemic influenza preparedness framework are to be shared among companies fairly and transparently, with amounts set by the Director-General with the Advisory Group. It also invites voluntary and in-kind contributions and urges continued support for laboratory and surveillance capacity in developing countries.

Opens the section on governance and review, stating that WHO oversees the framework through the World Health Assembly, the Director-General and an independent Advisory Group of international experts. It describes the Assembly's oversight role and begins to set out the Director-General's functions and the Advisory Group's mandate.

Describes how the Advisory Group is formed, with 18 members drawn from three Member States in each WHO region and balanced representation of developed and developing countries. It then begins the section on terms of reference for laboratories of WHO's global influenza surveillance and response system.

States that laboratory terms of reference will be reviewed regularly by the Director-General with the Advisory Group and others, and that Member States may report suspected non-compliance. It notes that the framework and its annexes are to be reviewed by 2016, with any proposals going to the Health Assembly in 2017.
A blank page with no extracted text.
A section divider page reading 'Annexes' in Russian.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Annex 1 presents the first standard material transfer agreement, covering exchanges of pandemic influenza biological materials within WHO's surveillance and response system. It limits the parties to WHO-designated or recognized influenza laboratories and defines the materials covered.

Sets out general provisions and the provider's obligations under the first transfer agreement, including following the system's terms of reference and national biosafety standards. It also covers the provider's consent to onward transfer and use of materials by other members of the system.

Continues the first transfer agreement with obligations to involve and credit scientists from originating laboratories and countries in research and publications. It states that neither party will seek intellectual property rights over the materials, and covers warranties and biosafety responsibilities.

Gives the agreement's duration, in force until the end of 2021 and automatically renewed to 2031 unless the Health Assembly decides otherwise. It explains that laboratories accept the agreement through their terms of reference or designation, and that no signature is needed unless a party asks for one.

Annex 2 presents the second standard material transfer agreement, between WHO and recipients outside the surveillance system, such as vaccine, diagnostics and pharmaceutical makers and research institutions. It sets out definitions and begins the recipient's obligations, chosen according to the nature and capacity of each recipient.

Lists options for recipients' commitments, such as donating or reserving at least 10% of real-time pandemic vaccine production for WHO, providing antivirals and granting licences to manufacturers in developing countries. Footnotes note that the vaccine share is flexible within a range of 5–20% in negotiations.

Continues the recipient options with diagnostic kits and support for laboratory capacity and technology transfer in developing countries, plus other contributions recipients should consider. It closes with provisions for settling disputes through negotiation or arbitration.

Covers the remaining articles of the second agreement, most of which are left for the parties to agree, and affirms that WHO's privileges and immunities are not waived. It ends with signature blocks for WHO and the recipient.

Annex 3 gives the terms of reference of the Advisory Group, adopted in 2008 and amended in 2011, and explains its origins in a 2007 intergovernmental statement on fair virus and benefit sharing. It lists the laboratories and parts of the system the group covers, noting that industry is not included though it may be consulted.

Sets out the Advisory Group's functions, centring on monitoring, assessing and reporting on how the framework operates. Items to monitor include timely sharing of H5N1 and other pandemic-potential viruses, the virus traceability mechanism, laboratory capacity and benefit sharing.

Describes how the 18 Advisory Group members are appointed, serving three-year terms with a third renewed each year and balanced representation of WHO regions. It also covers confidentiality and states that the Director-General will provide staff and funding for the group.

Annex 4 gives guiding principles for drawing up terms of reference for current and future laboratories in WHO's influenza surveillance system dealing with H5N1 and other pandemic viruses. It notes that roles differ by type of laboratory and begins listing the principles, such as compliance with the framework and transfer agreement.

Continues the guiding principles, which cover support for global health emergency response, rapid sharing of materials using the virus traceability mechanism, and timely submission of gene sequence data to public databases. Originating laboratories that supply materials must be properly credited.

Annex 5 opens the terms of reference for WHO collaborating centres for influenza, describing the surveillance system's role in global alerts and its four categories of laboratories coordinated by WHO's Global Influenza Programme. It notes that collaborating centres perform detailed analysis and select candidate vaccine viruses.

States that the agreed guiding principles govern all activities of the system's laboratories when acting in that role. It then reproduces the opening guiding principles for developing laboratory terms of reference.

Repeats the remaining guiding principles on sharing materials, submitting sequence data and crediting originating laboratories. It then begins listing collaborating centres' core terms of reference, including biosafety compliance.

Continues the collaborating centres' general duties, such as serving as a technical resource for WHO, crediting originating laboratories and keeping close links with national influenza centres. They must also alert WHO and source countries to unusual findings and train system laboratories in diagnostic methods.

Lists the collaborating centres' laboratory duties, including accurate typing and subtyping of influenza A(H5) and other pandemic-potential viruses and virus isolation in eggs and cell culture. They are also to carry out antigenic and genetic analysis, share gene sequences quickly and keep WHO informed about candidate vaccine viruses.

Continues the collaborating centres' duties with producing diagnostic reagents for national influenza centres and sharing specimens and viruses with other system laboratories under the transfer agreement. Partners include essential regulatory laboratories developing candidate vaccine viruses and potency reagents.

Requires collaborating centres to involve and credit scientists from originating countries in research and publications, and notes that specific terms of reference add functions based on each centre's expertise.

Opens the terms of reference for national influenza centres with the same background on the surveillance system's structure and four categories of laboratories. It states that the agreed guiding principles govern the work of all the system's laboratories.

Reproduces the guiding principles for laboratory terms of reference, covering compliance with the framework and transfer agreement, coordination with WHO and timely reporting of test results. It also covers support to Member States and crediting of originating laboratories.

Sets out the core terms of reference of national influenza centres, which are designated by health ministries and recognized by WHO. Their general duties include working under the Global Influenza Programme, using the virus traceability mechanism and complying with the transfer agreement.

Continues the national influenza centres' duties, such as sending hard-to-identify specimens to a WHO collaborating centre or H5 reference laboratory within one week, with relevant data. They should also attend training, strengthen national surveillance, advise other laboratories and credit contributors in publications.

Opens the terms of reference for WHO H5 reference laboratories with the standard background on the surveillance system and its four types of laboratories. It notes that the agreed guiding principles govern all their work as system laboratories.

Reproduces the guiding principles for laboratory terms of reference again, from compliance with the framework and transfer agreement to coordination with WHO and timely reporting. It continues through the principles on sharing materials and submitting gene sequence data.

Defines WHO H5 reference laboratories as those designated ad hoc by WHO and lists their general duties, such as meeting WHO criteria for confirming human infection and using the traceability mechanism. It begins their technical duties, starting with advising clinics and hospitals on safe specimen collection and transport.

Continues the H5 reference laboratories' duties, including accurate diagnosis and subtyping of A(H5) and other pandemic-potential viruses and expert support during outbreaks. They must also pass specimens and isolates to WHO collaborating centres, share gene sequences quickly and credit contributors in publications.

Opens the terms of reference for essential regulatory laboratories with the standard background on the surveillance system. It notes that these laboratories may carry out their core duties individually or as a group, with specific terms agreed with WHO and sometimes with industry.

States that the agreed guiding principles govern the work of all the system's laboratories and reproduces those principles. They include compliance with the transfer agreement, coordination with WHO, timely reporting and rapid sharing of materials.

Ends the guiding principles and begins the core terms of reference of essential regulatory laboratories. These include advising WHO on choosing H5N1 and other pandemic-potential viruses for vaccines and helping WHO and Member States with vaccine-related standards.

Continues the essential regulatory laboratories' duties, such as developing and characterizing candidate vaccine viruses at WHO's request, storing them and preparing calibrated reference reagents with other such laboratories. They are also to distribute these materials to interested laboratories and vaccine makers and to credit contributors in publications.

The back cover of the Russian edition, giving the ISBN and WHO's Geneva address.
